idiom_name: struct with interface ports + Database.BeginTx, tx passed to every port call
implementation_notes: The service is a struct with interface-typed ports; the use case begins the transaction with db.BeginTx, defers Rollback (a no-op after Commit) and passes the *sql.Tx - or the narrower DBTX interface that both *sql.DB and *sql.Tx satisfy, as sqlc generates - into every port method. There is no container and no declarative transaction: the composition root wires the struct and the unit of work becomes an explicit parameter. Typing the ports on a DBTX-style interface keeps database/sql out of the domain without adding a wrapper type.
pitfalls: defer tx.Rollback() must be registered immediately after BeginTx, before any early error return, or the connection keeps an open transaction.
Calling the pool's plain methods inside the use case silently runs outside the transaction; every port call must receive the tx handle.
Holding the transaction across HTTP calls to third parties is a common source of pool exhaustion and deadlocks in Go services.

variants.name: Callback transactor (unit-of-work port)
variants.idiom_name: uow.Execute(ctx, func(tx Store) error) - commits on nil, rolls back on error
variants.implementation_notes: Instead of threading *sql.Tx through every signature, the service depends on a small unit-of-work port whose Execute(ctx, fn) begins, commits or rolls back around the callback, and whose tx argument is a store interface implemented by both the pooled and the transactional store. The service layer then never imports database/sql, the same store type works inside and outside a transaction, and test doubles are trivial; the cost is one more abstraction and a callback nesting level.
pitfalls: A callback that swallows an error and returns nil commits the transaction; every failure path must return it.
Nested Execute calls must reuse the active transaction (through the context) or they deadlock waiting for a second connection.
The result must be captured in an outer variable, because the callback returns only an error.
